100	 The Impact of Non-Operative Hip and Core Injuries on National Football
101	
102	                     League Athlete Performance
103	
104	
105	
106	
107	                                                                         3
108	 Abstract
109	
110	Objectives: Hip and core injuries are common in National Football League (NFL) athletes;
111	
112	however, the impact following injury remains unclear. The goal of this manuscript is to
113	
114	determine the impact of nonoperative hip and core injuries on return to play and performance.
115	
116	Methods: NFL athletes who sustained a hip or core injury treated non-operatively between 2010-
117	
118	2016 were identified. Offensive and defensive power ratings were calculated for each player’s
119	
120	injury season and 2 seasons before and after to assess longitudinal impact. A matched control
121	
122	group without an identified hip and/or core injury were assembled for comparison.
123	
124	Results: A total of 41 offensive and 71 defensive players with nonoperative hip or core injury
125	
126	were analyzed. All athletes returned to play; offensive and defensive players missed 4.0 ± 5.2
127	
128	and 3.1 ± 2.6 games after injury, respectively. Offensive players played fewer cumulative career
129	
130	games returning from core injury versus hip (23.5 ± 20.6 vs 41.0 ± 26.4). Defensive players
131	
132	played fewer games (58.1 ± 41.1 versus 37.4 ± 27.1, p<0.05) with lower defensive power rating
133	
134	(133.9 ± 128.5 versus 219.8 ± 212.2, p<0.05) cumulatively after hip or core injury. Additionally,
135	
136	two years following injury, defensive players played fewer games compared to controls (9.5 ±
137	
138	7.0 versus 10.9 ± 6.8, p<0.05). Following hip injury specifically, NFL defenders played fewer
139	
140	games (39.8 ± 27.9 vs 61.9 ± 38.8; p<0.05) and had a lower defensive power rating (145.9 ±
141	
142	131.7 vs 239.0 ± 205.9; p<0.05) compared to before injury.
143	
144	Conclusion: Overall, NFL players return to play following nonoperative hip and core injuries.
145	
146	Defensive players played in fewer games following hip or core injury compared to controls;
147	
148	offensive players were unaffected. Hip injuries have a greater impact on performance compared
149	
150	to core injuries in defensive athletes; offensive players played fewer games upon return from
151	
152	core injury.
153	
154	                                                                                                 4
155	 Key Terms: Muscle injuries, football, groin pain, hip/pelvis/thigh, core
156	
157	
158	
159	
160	                                                                           5
161	 Introduction
162	
163	       Injuries in the National Football League (NFL) have been shown to have a significant
164	
165	financial burden to both players and organizations.[1, 2] A systematic review of athletes entering
166	
167	the NFL combine with a musculoskeletal injury that required orthopedic intervention are
168	
169	uniformly at risk for decreased performance and fewer games, the effects of which resonate
170	
171	throughout an NFL player’s career.[3, 4] Although knee and shoulder injury account for the
172	
173	highest incidence of time loss injuries among NFL players, they are at significant risk for injuries
174	
175	to other anatomic regions, particularly the hip and core.[5, 6, 7, 8]
176	
177	       Hip and core injuries in the NFL account for approximately 10% of NFL injuries; the
178	
179	majority are classified as muscle strains. [9, 10] In fact, hip flexor strains occurred 268 times
180	
181	over a 10 year period in the NFL, and were the most common hip injury. [10] Football players
182	
183	are particularly vulnerable to core injuries such as rib fractures or contusions, back stiffness as
184	
185	well as abdominal/oblique strains, and athletic pubalgia due to the physical nature of the game.
186	
187	[11, 12] Prior studies have examined the effect of surgical intervention on groin injuries,
188	
189	showing that operative intervention for athletica pubalgia led to significantly shorter career
190	
191	length and games per season compared to matched controls,[13] however the impact of
192	
193	nonoperative hip and core injuries on NFL player performance has not been elucidated.
194	
195	       The purpose of our investigation was to determine the impact of nonoperative hip and
196	
197	core injuries on the performance in NFL athletes. We sought to determine if these injuries had a
198	
199	significant impact on return to play rates, as well as offensive and defensive player productivity.
200	
201	It was hypothesized that both offensive and defensive NFL players who sustained a nonoperative
202	
203	hip or core injury would return to play but play fewer games and experience worse performance
204	
205	following their return as compared to healthy controls matched for age, position, and NFL
206	
207	experience.
208	                                                                                                      6
209	 Methods
210	
211	       Data were collected retrospectively for this study; internal review board exemption was
212	
213	granted since all material is freely accessible. All NFL players who sustained a hip or core injury
214	
215	between 2010-2016 seasons were collected from publicly available sources such as injury
216	
217	reports, player profiles, team pages and game summaries using methods previously utilized in
218	
219	other studies.[13, 14, 15, 16] Indexed hip injuries included adductor strain, hip flexor strain,
220	
221	labral tears, hip inflammation or impingement while core injuries included oblique, abdominal or
222	
223	intercostal strains, as well as back spasms or stiffness. Injuries were cross referenced with public
224	
225	websites including official team pages, official press releases, and personal player websites,
226	
227	using methodology that has been utilized by previous studies using publicly available
228	
229	databases.[13, 14, 15, 16] The NFL mandates that teams quickly and accurately disseminate
230	
231	injury information to the league office, their opponents, local and national media, and the team’s
232	
233	broadcast partners. Return-to-play (RTP) data was further confirmed by identifying gaps in
234	
235	reported statistics. Fractures, disc herniations, and any player who was reported to have
236	
237	undergone surgery for their injury were not included in the investigation.
238	
239	       Demographic data surrounding the injury were recorded such as BMI, age at injury,
240	
241	season in NFL that injury occurred and position. The total number of games played before and
242	
243	after the reported injury date were also recorded. Performance data was collected for each player
244	
245	including total games played, total yards (passing, rushing or receiving) and touchdowns for
246	
247	offensive players and total tackles, sacks and interceptions for defensive players. Offensive and
248	
249	defensive power ratings were also calculated from these variables, which have both been
250	
251	previously described and validated outcomes measures of a football player’s overall contribution
252	
253	to the team’s offense or defense.[14, 17, 18] They are calculated with the following formulas:
254	                                                                                                    7
255	 Offensive power rating (OPR) = [(total yards/10) + (touchdowns/6)]
256	
257	Defensive power rating (DPR) = [total tackles + (total sacks x 2) + (total interceptions x 2)]
258	
259	       Overall career data as well as data in the two years prior to and following the date of
260	
261	injury were collected in order to better assess longitudinal changes in performance. Power ratings
262	
263	are intended to calculate productivity over a season, not individual games; therefore, the
264	
265	individual statistics were also evaluated on a per game basis to account for games missed. A
266	
267	control group was assembled by 2:1 matching injured athletes with healthy rostered NFL players
268	
269	that did not sustain a documented hip and/or groin injury by age, position, performance data, and
270	
271	NFL experience within three seasons in accordance to previously established methodology. [13,
272	
273	14, 15] Control players were chosen based on an index date which was matched with the study
274	
275	player’s date of injury. This control group was established to compare performance before and
276	
277	after hip/core injury. Additionally, if players did not participate in the season prior to the index
278	
279	injury season they were excluded. Furthermore, athletes injured at the end of the season who
280	
281	were unable to return-to-play during the index season were excluded from the study. When
282	
283	calculating time missed from injury, bye weeks were not a factor, only the number of games
284	
285	missed. Power rating has been previously demonstrated in other investigations to be a valid and
286	
287	effective method for quantifying overall player performance;[14] however, since several studies
288	
289	demonstrated offensive power ratings are not an effective performance metric for offensive
290	
291	linemen (OL) or kickers (K), only offensive skill players (wide receivers [WR], running backs
292	
293	[RB], tight ends [TE], and quarterbacks [QB]) were included for offensive power ratings.[17, 18]
294	
295	Statistical Analysis
296	
297	       All continuous data are reported as mean ± standard deviation, while categorical data are
298	
299	reported as counts and column percentages. Comparisons between injured and control players
300	
301	
302	                                                                                                       8
303	 are performed using independent 2-sample t-tests for continuous variables and using chi-square
304	
305	tests for categorical variables. Comparisons between pre- and post- data are performed using
306	
307	paired t-tests if the variable is normally distributed, and Wilcoxon signed rank tests if the
308	
309	variable is non-normally distributed. Statistical significance is set at p<0.05. All analyses are
310	
311	performed using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).
312	
313	
314	
315	Results
316	
317	        A total of 112 (41 offensive and 71 defensive) NFL players were identified as having
318	
319	sustained a hip or core injury between 2010 and 2016 that also matched our inclusion criteria.
320	
321	The offensive group included 15 wide receivers, 10 offensive linemen, 6 tight ends, 5 running
322	
323	backs, 4 quarterbacks and 1 kicker. Defensive players included 33 defensive backs, 19
324	
325	linebackers, 10 defensive ends, and 9 defensive tackles. A 2:1 matched control group consisting
326	
327	of 224 players was compared to the study group and demonstrated no statistical differences in
328	
329	age, years of NFL experience, position, or BMI (Table 1). Pre-injury performance did not
330	
331	significantly differ between the injured group and healthy controls. No players sustained injuries
332	
333	requiring retirement.

494	
495	Discussion
496	
497	       The present investigation demonstrated a 100% return-to-play rate after hip or core injury
498	
499	for NFL players. Defensive players with a either a hip or core injury demonstrated significantly
500	
501	fewer games played and both offensive and defensive players experienced decreased power
502	
503	ratings post-injury compared to before injury. Compared to healthy controls, defensive athletes
504	
505	played in significantly fewer games in the two years following injury but returned to near
506	
507	baseline at long term career follow up. Defensive players who sustained hip injuries alone had
508	
509	significantly decreased games played and power ratings in their post-injury careers compared to
510	
511	prior. Offensive players who sustained a core injury had significantly fewer games played in
512	
513	their cumulative career following injury compared to healthy controls.
514	
515	       Hip and groin injuries occur frequently in football players and are a leading cause of
516	
517	injury and lost playing time during both practice and games. [19] In a descriptive epidemiologic
518	
519	study of 23,806 NFL injuries from 1997 to 2006, Feeley et al. found that injuries around the hip
520	
521	comprised 3.1% of total injuries, with muscle strains being the most common. Wide receivers
522	
523	(39.6% of offensive injuries) and defensive backs (47.1% of defensive injuries) were among the
524	
525	most affected by these injuries. [10] The present study found a nearly identical incidence of
526	
527	injury, with wide receivers accounting for 37% of offensive injuries and defensive backs 46% of
528	
529	defensive injuries, with all athletes able to RTP.
530	
531	       High rates of hip and groin injury have also been documented in National Collegiate
532	
533	Athletic Association (NCAA) football players. Kerbel et al reviewed the incidence of hip and
534	
535	groin injuries across multiple sports and found that football players sustained 62.7 hip or groin
536	                                                                                                    13
537	 injuries per 100,000 athlete exposures, with the majority of reported injuries to either the
538	
539	adductor or hip flexor musculature.[20] Specifically investigating muscular strains about the hip,
540	
541	Eckard et al reviewed groin injuries in NCAA athletes and found that hip flexor and adductor
542	
543	muscles strains occurred at a rate of 1.93 and 1.43 per 10,000 athletic exposures in football
544	
545	players, respectively.[21] The present cohort similarly revealed groin or hip flexor strain/tear as
546	
547	among the most common injury type, comprising 56.1% of offensive and 67.6% of defensive
548	
549	injuries. Eckard et al also found 7.4% and 6.9% recurrence rate of hip flexor and adductor strains
550	
551	during the study period, compared to 9.8% of all athletes in our cohort with a documented re-
552	
553	injury.[21] Adductor strains, specifically, have the potential to alter the mechanics of the anterior
554	
555	musculature about the hip leading to increased risk of future rectus strains or athletic
556	
557	pubalgia.[22] Adductor injuries have been shown to cause significant increases in missed time
558	
559	from sport in other professional leagues. Long term performance and career longevity, however,
560	
561	were not altered. [23] These findings suggest that although muscular strains may appear benign,
562	
563	athletes with these injuries are at risk for future strains and time away from sport. Considering
564	
565	groin injuries cause significant time missed in the NFL and other professional sports, prevention
566	
567	is worth investigating. A study by Tyler et al revealed a dedicated physical therapy program
568	
569	targeted at adductor strengthening was beneficial in decreasing the incidence of groin strains in
570	
571	National Hockey League players; a similar training regimen may be beneficial in the NFL as
572	
573	well. [24]
574	
575	       Little is known about the effect of nonoperative core injuries such as back spasm, core
576	
577	stiffness and oblique strain on NFL players. A study utilizing a convenience sample of 267
578	
579	NCAA football players with lumbar spine injuries found that 59.6% of athletes reporting
580	
581	muscular low back pain or contusion were able to return to sport in less than 24 hours and 72.6%
582	
583	
584	
585	                                                                                                    14
586	 of players who did not return in <24 hours returned within a week of injury.[25] Rebolledo et al
587	
588	examined 214 NFL athletes at the combine and found that 50% had a history of abdominal core
589	
590	or lower extremity muscular injury which was also associated with lower levels of Vitamin D.[9]
591	
592	The effect of back and core injury has also been examined in other professional sports, as Camp
593	
594	et al found that core and back injury accounted for 12% of injuries resulting in missed time in
595	
596	Major League Baseball (MLB).[26] Likewise, Marshall et al found that core injuries in MLB
597	
598	pitchers lead to 47.0 ± 5.6 days on the injured list with fewer strikeouts per nine innings in the
599	
600	year of injury.[16] In the our study, athletes sustaining a core injury missed an average of 4.8 ±
601	
602	5.9 games following these injuries and all athletes were able to RTP without significant
603	
604	performance detriment. Additionally, offensive players who suffered a core injury played
605	
606	significantly fewer games throughout the remainder of their post-injury career compared to
607	
608	healthy controls, which could be partially attributed to similarities in athletic demand between a
609	
610	quarterback and MLB pitcher. While return to play rates are high and the current literature does
611	
612	not report significant changes in football performance, Domb et al reviewed disability claims in
613	
614	retired NFL athletes and found that 63 of 65 former players reported symptomatic lumbar spine
615	
616	strain. [27] It is important to note that, while core, and more specifically lumbar spine strains
617	
618	may not be associated with any surgical pathology, the repetitive stress can have implications on
619	
620	the future health of the athlete.
621	
622	        Specifically evaluating hip injuries in the NFL, Feeley et al noted that athletes lost an
623	
624	average of 12.3 days, with a median loss time of 4 days following a variety of hip injuries, such
625	
626	as muscle strains, contusions, and intra-articular pathology.[10] In the aforementioned study by
627	
628	Marshall et al, pitchers with hip injuries spent an average of 37.7 ± 8.1 days on the injured list
629	
630	and starting pitchers suffered from decreased fastball velocity during their initial season
631	
632	
633	                                                                                                     15
634	 following injury.[16] Additionally, injuries around the hip joint have also been shown to lead to
635	
636	missed time in professional basketball, as Jackson et al reviewed 24 years of data and found that
637	
638	hip injury accounted for 14.6% of all athletic injuries and lead to an average of 6.3 ± 10.2 days
639	
640	missed. [28] In our investigation, defensive players were more affected by hip injury than core
641	
642	injuries, with individual decreases in DPR following a hip injury but not a core injury, as well as
643	
644	fewer games played in the two years following injury compared to healthy controls.
645	
646	       Although both offensive skilled players and defensive players saw a decrease in power
647	
648	ratings compared to their own previous performance, neither group experienced a significant
649	
650	decline in performance compared to the control group following a hip or core injury. In a 2017
651	
652	review of player injuries at the NFL combine, Beaulieu-Jones et al. demonstrated that among
653	
654	NFL athletes entering the draft, defensive players with an injury history played fewer games in
655	
656	their first two years in the league compared to healthy controls (22.2 ± 7.9 vs 24.2 ± 7.6 games;
657	
658	p=0.001). Similarly, our study demonstrated that defensive players who suffered a hip or core
659	
660	injury played in fewer games the two years following compared to healthy defensive controls.
661	
662	Additionally, a systematic review by Wang et al looked at 32 studies pertaining to injury
663	
664	surveillance and monitoring at the NFL combine and found that overall, defensive linemen and
665	
666	defensive backs appeared to have their game participation most affected by an injury history
667	
668	compared to offensive athletes.[3] This is likely due to the inherently violent nature of defensive
669	
670	play as compared to offensive play, which predisposes defensive players to more energy transfer
671	
672	and higher impact, and thus higher injury rate. The defensive back position involves more
673	
674	efficient energy transfer in the kinetic chain during movements like backpedaling, quick
675	
676	reactionary changes in direction, and regular high-speed contact, which may help to explain the
677	
678	higher incidence of hip injuries among defensive players. However, it is important to note that in
679	
680	
681	                                                                                                    16
682	 the present investigation performance decline following an injury was not significantly different
683	
684	for offensive skilled or defensive players when comparing to matched controls, thus while
685	
686	athletes may expect some decrease in individual performance, it will not statistically exceed
687	
688	other NFL players of similar age and position.
689	
690	       Our study is not without limitations. Player injury reports were collected from publicly
691	
692	available internet sources which may be subject to inaccuracies. However, the NFL mandates
693	
694	that teams provide accurate and prompt injury information to the league as well as the media.
695	
696	Similar to previous investigations, injuries reports were confirmed with additional publicly
697	
698	available injury reports. [13, 14, 15] With pressure to stay in the game and continue playing,
699	
700	these injuries may also be unreported, as players might not disclose injuries to the team, medical
701	
702	staff and media. Furthermore, while game statistics are an important indicator of player
703	
704	performance, there are many unmeasured contributions not captured, thus true “performance” of
705	
706	a player cannot be completely summarized by these statistics alone. Our use of player power
707	
708	rating attempts to mitigate this issue by generating a weighted value that emphasizes commonly
709	
710	agreed upon significant performance variables.[17] These power ratings, however, do not
711	
712	capture kicker or offensive linemen contributions, therefore these players were excluded from
713	
714	power rating analysis. In addition, hip and core injuries include a broad spectrum of pathologies,
715	
716	and public injury reports often do not indicate the specific diagnosis. We are unable to access
717	
718	clinical exam findings, subjective reports from the athlete, imaging results, and attempted
719	
720	conservative treatment modalities. Future studies should aim to identify specific features that
721	
722	favor successful nonoperative management of common hip and core injuries and correlate with
723	
724	performance.
725	
726	
727	
728	Conclusion
729	                                                                                                  17
730	        Overall, 100% of NFL players in our study returned to play following nonoperative hip
731	
732	and core injuries. Defensive players were more affected post-injury compared to offensive
733	
734	players. Hip injuries have a greater impact on performance compared to core injuries in
735	
736	defensive athletes; offensive athletes played fewer games upon return from core injury but were
737	
738	able to maintain their performance. At long term follow up, both offensive and defensive players
739	
740	were able to return to near baseline games played and power ratings.

                                                                                              2
 The Impact of Non-Operative Hip and Core Injuries on National Football

                     League Athlete Performance




                                                                         3
 Abstract

Objectives: Hip and core injuries are common in National Football League (NFL) athletes;

however, the impact following injury remains unclear. The goal of this manuscript is to

determine the impact of nonoperative hip and core injuries on return to play and performance.

Methods: NFL athletes who sustained a hip or core injury treated non-operatively between 2010-

2016 were identified. Offensive and defensive power ratings were calculated for each player’s

injury season and 2 seasons before and after to assess longitudinal impact. A matched control

group without an identified hip and/or core injury were assembled for comparison.

Results: A total of 41 offensive and 71 defensive players with nonoperative hip or core injury

were analyzed. All athletes returned to play; offensive and defensive players missed 4.0 ± 5.2

and 3.1 ± 2.6 games after injury, respectively. Offensive players played fewer cumulative career

games returning from core injury versus hip (23.5 ± 20.6 vs 41.0 ± 26.4). Defensive players

played fewer games (58.1 ± 41.1 versus 37.4 ± 27.1, p<0.05) with lower defensive power rating

(133.9 ± 128.5 versus 219.8 ± 212.2, p<0.05) cumulatively after hip or core injury. Additionally,

two years following injury, defensive players played fewer games compared to controls (9.5 ±

7.0 versus 10.9 ± 6.8, p<0.05). Following hip injury specifically, NFL defenders played fewer

games (39.8 ± 27.9 vs 61.9 ± 38.8; p<0.05) and had a lower defensive power rating (145.9 ±

131.7 vs 239.0 ± 205.9; p<0.05) compared to before injury.

Conclusion: Overall, NFL players return to play following nonoperative hip and core injuries.

Defensive players played in fewer games following hip or core injury compared to controls;

offensive players were unaffected. Hip injuries have a greater impact on performance compared

to core injuries in defensive athletes; offensive players played fewer games upon return from

core injury.

                                                                                                 4
 Key Terms: Muscle injuries, football, groin pain, hip/pelvis/thigh, core




                                                                           5
 Introduction

       Injuries in the National Football League (NFL) have been shown to have a significant

financial burden to both players and organizations.[1, 2] A systematic review of athletes entering

the NFL combine with a musculoskeletal injury that required orthopedic intervention are

uniformly at risk for decreased performance and fewer games, the effects of which resonate

throughout an NFL player’s career.[3, 4] Although knee and shoulder injury account for the

highest incidence of time loss injuries among NFL players, they are at significant risk for injuries

to other anatomic regions, particularly the hip and core.[5, 6, 7, 8]

       Hip and core injuries in the NFL account for approximately 10% of NFL injuries; the

majority are classified as muscle strains. [9, 10] In fact, hip flexor strains occurred 268 times

over a 10 year period in the NFL, and were the most common hip injury. [10] Football players

are particularly vulnerable to core injuries such as rib fractures or contusions, back stiffness as

well as abdominal/oblique strains, and athletic pubalgia due to the physical nature of the game.

[11, 12] Prior studies have examined the effect of surgical intervention on groin injuries,

showing that operative intervention for athletica pubalgia led to significantly shorter career

length and games per season compared to matched controls,[13] however the impact of

nonoperative hip and core injuries on NFL player performance has not been elucidated.

       The purpose of our investigation was to determine the impact of nonoperative hip and

core injuries on the performance in NFL athletes. We sought to determine if these injuries had a

significant impact on return to play rates, as well as offensive and defensive player productivity.

It was hypothesized that both offensive and defensive NFL players who sustained a nonoperative

hip or core injury would return to play but play fewer games and experience worse performance

following their return as compared to healthy controls matched for age, position, and NFL

experience.
                                                                                                      6
 Methods

       Data were collected retrospectively for this study; internal review board exemption was

granted since all material is freely accessible. All NFL players who sustained a hip or core injury

between 2010-2016 seasons were collected from publicly available sources such as injury

reports, player profiles, team pages and game summaries using methods previously utilized in

other studies.[13, 14, 15, 16] Indexed hip injuries included adductor strain, hip flexor strain,

labral tears, hip inflammation or impingement while core injuries included oblique, abdominal or

intercostal strains, as well as back spasms or stiffness. Injuries were cross referenced with public

websites including official team pages, official press releases, and personal player websites,

using methodology that has been utilized by previous studies using publicly available

databases.[13, 14, 15, 16] The NFL mandates that teams quickly and accurately disseminate

injury information to the league office, their opponents, local and national media, and the team’s

broadcast partners. Return-to-play (RTP) data was further confirmed by identifying gaps in

reported statistics. Fractures, disc herniations, and any player who was reported to have

undergone surgery for their injury were not included in the investigation.

       Demographic data surrounding the injury were recorded such as BMI, age at injury,

season in NFL that injury occurred and position. The total number of games played before and

after the reported injury date were also recorded. Performance data was collected for each player

including total games played, total yards (passing, rushing or receiving) and touchdowns for

offensive players and total tackles, sacks and interceptions for defensive players. Offensive and

defensive power ratings were also calculated from these variables, which have both been

previously described and validated outcomes measures of a football player’s overall contribution

to the team’s offense or defense.[14, 17, 18] They are calculated with the following formulas:
                                                                                                    7
 Offensive power rating (OPR) = [(total yards/10) + (touchdowns/6)]

Defensive power rating (DPR) = [total tackles + (total sacks x 2) + (total interceptions x 2)]

       Overall career data as well as data in the two years prior to and following the date of

injury were collected in order to better assess longitudinal changes in performance. Power ratings

are intended to calculate productivity over a season, not individual games; therefore, the

individual statistics were also evaluated on a per game basis to account for games missed. A

control group was assembled by 2:1 matching injured athletes with healthy rostered NFL players

that did not sustain a documented hip and/or groin injury by age, position, performance data, and

NFL experience within three seasons in accordance to previously established methodology. [13,

14, 15] Control players were chosen based on an index date which was matched with the study

player’s date of injury. This control group was established to compare performance before and

after hip/core injury. Additionally, if players did not participate in the season prior to the index

injury season they were excluded. Furthermore, athletes injured at the end of the season who

were unable to return-to-play during the index season were excluded from the study. When

calculating time missed from injury, bye weeks were not a factor, only the number of games

missed. Power rating has been previously demonstrated in other investigations to be a valid and

effective method for quantifying overall player performance;[14] however, since several studies

demonstrated offensive power ratings are not an effective performance metric for offensive

linemen (OL) or kickers (K), only offensive skill players (wide receivers [WR], running backs

[RB], tight ends [TE], and quarterbacks [QB]) were included for offensive power ratings.[17, 18]

Statistical Analysis

       All continuous data are reported as mean ± standard deviation, while categorical data are

reported as counts and column percentages. Comparisons between injured and control players


                                                                                                       8
 are performed using independent 2-sample t-tests for continuous variables and using chi-square

tests for categorical variables. Comparisons between pre- and post- data are performed using

paired t-tests if the variable is normally distributed, and Wilcoxon signed rank tests if the

variable is non-normally distributed. Statistical significance is set at p<0.05. All analyses are

performed using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).



Results

        A total of 112 (41 offensive and 71 defensive) NFL players were identified as having

sustained a hip or core injury between 2010 and 2016 that also matched our inclusion criteria.

The offensive group included 15 wide receivers, 10 offensive linemen, 6 tight ends, 5 running

backs, 4 quarterbacks and 1 kicker. Defensive players included 33 defensive backs, 19

linebackers, 10 defensive ends, and 9 defensive tackles. A 2:1 matched control group consisting

of 224 players was compared to the study group and demonstrated no statistical differences in

age, years of NFL experience, position, or BMI (Table 1). Pre-injury performance did not

significantly differ between the injured group and healthy controls. No players sustained injuries

requiring retirement.

Following hip injury, defensive athletes played in fewer games (39.8 ± 27.9 vs 61.9 ± 38.8;

P<0.05) and had a lower defensive rating (145.9 ± 131.7 vs 239.0 ± 205.9; P<0.05) compared to

their career before injury. Conversely, offensive skilled players experienced a significant

decrease in power rating compared to their career before injury (395.4 ± 567.4 vs 190.1 ± 327.6;

P<0.05). When compared to controls, both offensive skilled players and defensive players with




                                                                                                         12
 either hip or core injuries did not experience a significant decrease in cumulative career power

ratings following injury.



Discussion

       The present investigation demonstrated a 100% return-to-play rate after hip or core injury

for NFL players. Defensive players with a either a hip or core injury demonstrated significantly

fewer games played and both offensive and defensive players experienced decreased power

ratings post-injury compared to before injury. Compared to healthy controls, defensive athletes

played in significantly fewer games in the two years following injury but returned to near

baseline at long term career follow up. Defensive players who sustained hip injuries alone had

significantly decreased games played and power ratings in their post-injury careers compared to

prior. Offensive players who sustained a core injury had significantly fewer games played in

their cumulative career following injury compared to healthy controls.

       Hip and groin injuries occur frequently in football players and are a leading cause of

injury and lost playing time during both practice and games. [19] In a descriptive epidemiologic

study of 23,806 NFL injuries from 1997 to 2006, Feeley et al. found that injuries around the hip

comprised 3.1% of total injuries, with muscle strains being the most common. Wide receivers

(39.6% of offensive injuries) and defensive backs (47.1% of defensive injuries) were among the

most affected by these injuries. [10] The present study found a nearly identical incidence of

injury, with wide receivers accounting for 37% of offensive injuries and defensive backs 46% of

defensive injuries, with all athletes able to RTP.

       High rates of hip and groin injury have also been documented in National Collegiate

Athletic Association (NCAA) football players. Kerbel et al reviewed the incidence of hip and

groin injuries across multiple sports and found that football players sustained 62.7 hip or groin
                                                                                                    13
 injuries per 100,000 athlete exposures, with the majority of reported injuries to either the

adductor or hip flexor musculature.[20] Specifically investigating muscular strains about the hip,

Eckard et al reviewed groin injuries in NCAA athletes and found that hip flexor and adductor

muscles strains occurred at a rate of 1.93 and 1.43 per 10,000 athletic exposures in football

players, respectively.[21] The present cohort similarly revealed groin or hip flexor strain/tear as

among the most common injury type, comprising 56.1% of offensive and 67.6% of defensive

injuries. Eckard et al also found 7.4% and 6.9% recurrence rate of hip flexor and adductor strains

during the study period, compared to 9.8% of all athletes in our cohort with a documented re-

injury.[21] Adductor strains, specifically, have the potential to alter the mechanics of the anterior

musculature about the hip leading to increased risk of future rectus strains or athletic

pubalgia.[22] Adductor injuries have been shown to cause significant increases in missed time

from sport in other professional leagues. Long term performance and career longevity, however,

were not altered. [23] These findings suggest that although muscular strains may appear benign,

athletes with these injuries are at risk for future strains and time away from sport. Considering

groin injuries cause significant time missed in the NFL and other professional sports, prevention

is worth investigating. A study by Tyler et al revealed a dedicated physical therapy program

targeted at adductor strengthening was beneficial in decreasing the incidence of groin strains in

National Hockey League players; a similar training regimen may be beneficial in the NFL as

well. [24]

       Little is known about the effect of nonoperative core injuries such as back spasm, core

stiffness and oblique strain on NFL players. A study utilizing a convenience sample of 267

NCAA football players with lumbar spine injuries found that 59.6% of athletes reporting

muscular low back pain or contusion were able to return to sport in less than 24 hours and 72.6%



                                                                                                    14
 of players who did not return in <24 hours returned within a week of injury.[25] Rebolledo et al

examined 214 NFL athletes at the combine and found that 50% had a history of abdominal core

or lower extremity muscular injury which was also associated with lower levels of Vitamin D.[9]

The effect of back and core injury has also been examined in other professional sports, as Camp

et al found that core and back injury accounted for 12% of injuries resulting in missed time in

Major League Baseball (MLB).[26] Likewise, Marshall et al found that core injuries in MLB

pitchers lead to 47.0 ± 5.6 days on the injured list with fewer strikeouts per nine innings in the

year of injury.[16] In the our study, athletes sustaining a core injury missed an average of 4.8 ±

5.9 games following these injuries and all athletes were able to RTP without significant

performance detriment. Additionally, offensive players who suffered a core injury played

significantly fewer games throughout the remainder of their post-injury career compared to

healthy controls, which could be partially attributed to similarities in athletic demand between a

quarterback and MLB pitcher. While return to play rates are high and the current literature does

not report significant changes in football performance, Domb et al reviewed disability claims in

retired NFL athletes and found that 63 of 65 former players reported symptomatic lumbar spine

strain. [27] It is important to note that, while core, and more specifically lumbar spine strains

may not be associated with any surgical pathology, the repetitive stress can have implications on

the future health of the athlete.

        Specifically evaluating hip injuries in the NFL, Feeley et al noted that athletes lost an

average of 12.3 days, with a median loss time of 4 days following a variety of hip injuries, such

as muscle strains, contusions, and intra-articular pathology.[10] In the aforementioned study by

Marshall et al, pitchers with hip injuries spent an average of 37.7 ± 8.1 days on the injured list

and starting pitchers suffered from decreased fastball velocity during their initial season


                                                                                                     15
 following injury.[16] Additionally, injuries around the hip joint have also been shown to lead to

missed time in professional basketball, as Jackson et al reviewed 24 years of data and found that

hip injury accounted for 14.6% of all athletic injuries and lead to an average of 6.3 ± 10.2 days

missed. [28] In our investigation, defensive players were more affected by hip injury than core

injuries, with individual decreases in DPR following a hip injury but not a core injury, as well as

fewer games played in the two years following injury compared to healthy controls.

       Although both offensive skilled players and defensive players saw a decrease in power

ratings compared to their own previous performance, neither group experienced a significant

decline in performance compared to the control group following a hip or core injury. In a 2017

review of player injuries at the NFL combine, Beaulieu-Jones et al. demonstrated that among

NFL athletes entering the draft, defensive players with an injury history played fewer games in

their first two years in the league compared to healthy controls (22.2 ± 7.9 vs 24.2 ± 7.6 games;

p=0.001). Similarly, our study demonstrated that defensive players who suffered a hip or core

injury played in fewer games the two years following compared to healthy defensive controls.

Additionally, a systematic review by Wang et al looked at 32 studies pertaining to injury

surveillance and monitoring at the NFL combine and found that overall, defensive linemen and

defensive backs appeared to have their game participation most affected by an injury history

compared to offensive athletes.[3] This is likely due to the inherently violent nature of defensive

play as compared to offensive play, which predisposes defensive players to more energy transfer

and higher impact, and thus higher injury rate. The defensive back position involves more

efficient energy transfer in the kinetic chain during movements like backpedaling, quick

reactionary changes in direction, and regular high-speed contact, which may help to explain the

higher incidence of hip injuries among defensive players. However, it is important to note that in


                                                                                                    16
 the present investigation performance decline following an injury was not significantly different

for offensive skilled or defensive players when comparing to matched controls, thus while

athletes may expect some decrease in individual performance, it will not statistically exceed

other NFL players of similar age and position.

       Our study is not without limitations. Player injury reports were collected from publicly

available internet sources which may be subject to inaccuracies. However, the NFL mandates

that teams provide accurate and prompt injury information to the league as well as the media.

Similar to previous investigations, injuries reports were confirmed with additional publicly

available injury reports. [13, 14, 15] With pressure to stay in the game and continue playing,

these injuries may also be unreported, as players might not disclose injuries to the team, medical

staff and media. Furthermore, while game statistics are an important indicator of player

performance, there are many unmeasured contributions not captured, thus true “performance” of

a player cannot be completely summarized by these statistics alone. Our use of player power

rating attempts to mitigate this issue by generating a weighted value that emphasizes commonly

agreed upon significant performance variables.[17] These power ratings, however, do not

capture kicker or offensive linemen contributions, therefore these players were excluded from

power rating analysis. In addition, hip and core injuries include a broad spectrum of pathologies,

and public injury reports often do not indicate the specific diagnosis. We are unable to access

clinical exam findings, subjective reports from the athlete, imaging results, and attempted

conservative treatment modalities. Future studies should aim to identify specific features that

favor successful nonoperative management of common hip and core injuries and correlate with

performance.



Conclusion
                                                                                                  17
        Overall, 100% of NFL players in our study returned to play following nonoperative hip

and core injuries. Defensive players were more affected post-injury compared to offensive

players. Hip injuries have a greater impact on performance compared to core injuries in

defensive athletes; offensive athletes played fewer games upon return from core injury but were

able to maintain their performance. At long term follow up, both offensive and defensive players

were able to return to near baseline games played and power ratings.
